text: When a large number of correlated names (same sector) all line up at the same technical spot (resistance, EMAs, VWAP) on the same day, that alignment itself is read as an edge/signal from the market, not just a collection of individually good-looking charts.

Avoid chasing an extended sector/stock into strength even when the long-term trend looks bullish; the more extended a name is, the higher the odds of a pause or pullback, so wait for sideways consolidation before entering.

Extension can be judged visually (e.g., percent distance above the 9/50 EMA) without needing a formal indicator (ADR, distance-from-moving-average, etc.) - a systematic extension indicator is not a must.
Be wary of shorting a weak stock sitting inside an otherwise strong sector - relative weakness within strength is a lower-quality setup than weakness confirmed across the group.

No hard rule to move a stop to breakeven; exits are usually either the original stop getting hit, selling into strength, or a discretionary manual close when price action starts behaving abnormally relative to the trend.
There is no fixed definition for 'selling into strength' - you can't reliably nail the top, so this exit is discretionary by nature.

When trailing a winning trend trade, raise the stop to a structural level (e.g., an hourly 50 EMA) selectively after a confirming event like a breakout - not as a default rule - and use a level where a break below signals the uptrend is genuinely over.
Prefer sitting in winners over rotating capital between positions; the big money is made by staying with what's working (echoing Livermore).
Size down and use unusually tight stops (as low as ~0.5% price stop / ~0.15% account risk) on core large positions as account size grows, to keep slippage manageable at scale.

Using margin isn't the root cause of large drawdowns - revenge trading (increasing risk size after a loss) causes big drawdowns with or without leverage. The real skill is controlling the impulse to revenge trade, not simply avoiding margin.
Size smaller in smaller-cap or less-liquid names; typical position sizing runs about 20-25% of the account, and sizing much above ~35% into one name is treated as an outlier, not the norm.

Reserve outsized position sizing (well above normal, e.g. 30%+) for rare, high-conviction 'once in a decade' setups (e.g., a parabolic blow-off short), and treat these explicitly as exceptions rather than a template to repeat casually.
Historically (post-2008), corrections of 15-20%+ in the Nasdaq have started with relative weakness in the Russell 2000 - a necessary but not sufficient warning sign, not a standalone sell signal.

A market where mega-caps and large-cap software/tech grind steadily higher while small caps and speculative names break down is a narrow, selective-market pattern reminiscent of late-2021 topping action - worth noting as a risk context, not a definitive top call.
Treat scheduled macro news/Fed-speech days like any other trading day and react only to price action on the charts rather than trying to interpret the commentary itself.
Don't accept another trader's methods on faith - verify borrowed ideas yourself by 'flipping the charts'; a technique that works for one trader may not work for you.

When evaluating trading educators/content creators, a demonstrated track record of at least 2, preferably 3+, years is a useful filter to separate credible traders from unverified or marketing-driven content.
A gap-up that pushes stocks into overhead resistance rather than through it can itself be read as a potential short setup, rather than a bullish signal.
On an unclear/skeptical gap-up day, avoid being aggressive and instead just observe whether the market can follow through to the upside with broadening breadth before committing capital.
In an uptrend, a true market-leader stock will usually find support and bounce off the weekly EMA9 pullback -- he is always watching for a tight-risk entry near the weekly 9 on leadership names.

Chart review process: check the daily chart first; if the daily looks weak but the weekly is still in a strong uptrend (weekly 50 EMA trending higher, higher highs/higher lows intact), switch to the weekly chart to find a key level -- a weekly EMA or a candle low -- to trade off instead of dismissing the name.

A valid parabolic-short candidate needs a large enough move, clear volume expansion, and visible extension even on a lower timeframe (e.g. 60-minute); a move of only ~70% with no volume expansion and a recent pausing day is not extended enough to short.

When choosing between multiple good setups in the same sector, the general preference is liquidity and speed of movement -- compare ADR and dollar volume first, then finer technical details like undercut-and-rally patterns or inside-day volatility contraction.
Trade frequency should not be dictated by account/fund size -- it depends on your trading style, your timeframes, and which entry tactics or setups you actually use.

The goal of a speculator is to 'suck less' -- protect your downside first so you buy yourself time to develop your upside; focusing on upside while ignoring downside protection means one drawdown can wipe you out.
He lets his stop-losses work rather than trying to outsmart them -- about 95-99% of the time he does not cut a position before it hits his stop; cutting early happens, but it's rare.

The easiest way to avoid being affected by social-media noise about stocks/markets is to remove yourself from the environments that produce it -- he deleted Twitter and other trading-related apps for months when he judged they were hurting his trading.
His biggest historical mistakes, and what he most improved: making fewer random trades, not abandoning his stops, and not revenge-trading with increased risk after a loss.

He sees no need to justify sticking with his discretionary style -- it already suits him and has delivered good performance over the years, so the burden of proof is on switching styles, not on staying with what works.
When you don't have a strong opinion on market direction, it's fine to step back and trade less rather than forcing entries.

After a drawdown, rotate your posture: get more aggressive about taking profits on winners and more defensive/patient about new entries, adapting to your own equity curve performance, not just to the market.
When you're doing well, you tend to stop playing your A-game - success itself breeds a drop in discipline, so stay alert right after a hot streak.
A recurring personal mistake is getting into high-conviction trade ideas too early, before the real move starts; losing focus on a strong theme while chasing other setups compounds the problem.
Stick to your predefined stop (e.g. the day low) instead of exiting early on discretion - an early, emotional exit can cost you the entire move that a mechanical stop would have kept you in for.

Fast-moving assets like crypto don't give you time to wait for confirmation after the breakout is obvious - you have to anticipate the move and plan the trade before the prior swing high/base actually breaks.

Every ticker or asset class has its own character/behavior pattern - study how a specific name tends to move and adapt your approach to that character rather than applying one generic playbook to everything.

The first bounce after a parabolic climax run typically has a low win rate for real follow-through or a V-shaped recovery - it usually needs a second leg down or a sideways chop first before the next real uptrend starts.
Entries based on lower time frames have a higher failure rate ('fair trades') - cutting down on those and focusing more on daily-level signals raises overall trade quality.
Being too heavily leveraged forces you to give up good positions/opportunities early just to control drawdown - position sizing discipline matters more than conviction in a name.
Cap max drawdown from peak equity (e.g. keep it below roughly 20%) as a hard rule, but accept that holding larger positions for longer swings will sometimes produce bigger drawdowns as the trade-off.
A gap down against a fresh position is part of the game - let the stop execute at the open rather than trying to intervene; there's nothing you can do about it in the moment.
It's fine to skip a trade entirely when the market or a specific setup is choppy/undecided - wait to see whether support actually holds before committing.

When the broader market (e.g. Nasdaq/QQQ) has just recovered from a pullback or correction, that recovery is a good time to shift toward position trading your stocks rather than quick in-and-out trades.

For pullback buys, keep a mental watchlist of strong names and manually watch for price to pull back into a rising key EMA (9/21) or another support level in the coming days, rather than relying on pre-set price alerts.

When waiting to buy a dip in a sector or stock, don't just buy the first move down - wait for a decisive breakdown below a key level (e.g. anchored VWAP) followed by a support reaction or bounce before entering.

A strong rebound off a correction low that reclaims and holds above all key EMAs, combined with outsized trading volume relative to the stock's market cap, signals smart-money/institutional interest and is a bullish setup worth watching.
Trust your stops rather than trying to override or second-guess them with a discretionary read of price action in the moment.

Rather than defining an exit as a daily close below a certain EMA (which forces you to wait for the close), set a hard stop slightly below that EMA - or an equivalent EMA on a lower timeframe (e.g. a 150 EMA on the 60-min chart approximating a daily 21 or 200 EMA) - so the stop can trigger intraday.
An alternative stop-placement approach: place the stop below a recent candle's low, ideally one that also happens to sit slightly below a key EMA, rather than below the EMA alone.

An oversized single position can tie up so much buying power that it blocks you from entering other setups you actually want to take - a reason to be mindful of position sizing relative to available capital.
You will never nail the entry on every opportunity, and there will always be trades you miss entirely - don't dwell on or feel bad about the ones that got away.

The exact EMA/SMA period you use matters less than the fact that you've tested and compared it yourself and have conviction in why you use it - don't blindly copy another trader's indicator settings without doing your own study.

A stock that gaps down (or opens) into rising EMAs (support) is a much safer, higher-odds entry than one gapping up into a declining EMA or overhead resistance — the latter has a much higher chance of getting rejected and reversing.

Set your stop well below resistance rather than entering right at the highs into that resistance — that way even a mild pullback doesn't stop you out, whereas entering at the highs means normal chop can shake you out before the move even starts.
It's never wrong to book some profits and sell into strength, especially once a position is extended from a key moving average and approaching a prior swing high.
Small/micro caps are hard to trade and prone to shakeouts and fakeouts; with enough liquid, high-ADR mid-cap-and-above names available, there's no need to bother trading small caps.
The best pullback entries are the ones where multiple support levels — e.g. weekly 9 EMA, daily 9/21 EMA, 1-hour 50 EMA, and the prior breakout area — all converge at the same price.

Stops are only executed at the open, not pre-market or after-hours — if a stock gaps below the stop overnight, he lets it happen and reassesses the position/stop at the open rather than acting on the pre-market print.

Tightening a stop (holding all else equal) doesn't inherently change a trade's expectancy on its own, but in his experience the larger risk-multiple gained from a tighter stop tends to outweigh the decrease in win rate, because good trades rarely pull back more than ~1-1.5% before continuing in his favor.

There's no single best or 'magical' approach that works for everyone in trading; learn from what other traders share, but adapt or discard it based on what actually works for you rather than copying it 100%.

Avoids running a trading community/Discord because roughly 95% of trader-to-trader discussion is noise from people still in their learning phase; only a small fraction of experienced, profitable traders are actively engaged in group discussions.
Less screen time can be a net positive — you'll miss some trades, but you also cut out boredom trades and revenge trades, and can hold positions for longer.
A pullback that doesn't even touch the 9 EMA, while holding a prior breakout gap, is a sign of immense underlying strength.
Uses the 9 EMA as the objective level/guide for deciding whether to stay in or exit volatile (e.g. crypto) positions.
The number of positions held is irrelevant on its own -- what matters is market breadth, individual stock action, and the indices, not a fixed position count.
Don't try to outsmart or second-guess the market -- in a strong market, price can run much further than expected; let the market signal when it no longer wants to go up.
Avoid names where volume is too low relative to market cap -- expect a wide spread in the first 5-15 minutes of trading on such names.
Whether to require taking out the opening-range high on the 1-minute vs. 5-minute chart depends on where the market opens and how extended it is intraday.
When a stock approaches a declining resistance moving average (e.g. the 50 EMA), watch how price reacts there -- no rejection and a clean push through is a sign of strength.
Don't rely on charts alone -- line up the market, the sector, and the individual stock's context/rationale together; being obsessed with the chart in isolation loses a big part of the edge.
Index/sector context matters a lot for timing entries and improving win rate, but it isn't 'all about' the index -- individual stock selection and pattern still matter a great deal.
When comparing two similar names in the same group, prefer the relatively stronger one (e.g. choosing MU over SNDK).
Core trading philosophy: focus on getting entries with the tightest possible risk right before a range expansion.
Getting stopped out repeatedly (washed out) on the same names is a signal to go back and study whether entries or stop placement need improvement.

How much to trim into an earnings gap-risk event should be sized to the adverse gap you can psychologically/financially accept -- the more profit cushion, the less you need to trim; it's never wrong to book some profit.
Overexposure is subjective -- it's defined by what the individual trader can personally tolerate losing, not by an external rule on position count.

Build pattern recognition by studying past trades (especially shakeout entries) for real hours of work; if it still doesn't click after genuine effort, that entry style may simply not be a fit -- and that's fine.

Pick the breakout timeframe (1-minute vs. 5-minute vs. 15-minute) based on the stop size it implies -- a wider range on a longer timeframe means a wider percentage stop, so use a finer timeframe to keep risk tight.
Prefer buying a pullback to the rising 9 EMA (daily) or 50 EMA (intraday) over chasing an inside-day breakout, especially in stocks that habitually pull back after breaking out.

Small-cap stocks are harder to trade than liquid large caps: they get shaken out more often and rarely sustain multi-week/multi-month trends (mostly quick, explosive, hard-to-time runs), so trade them less and prioritize liquidity first.
A stock closing back above its key EMAs (the 9, and ideally the 21, on both daily and weekly) marks the first step of a character/trend change worth watching.
A candle that opens lower, pushes lower intraday, then reverses and closes at/near the highs is a strong bullish signal, especially when confirmed on both daily and weekly timeframes.
When most watchlist stocks are extended from the 9 EMA and running into resistance on a given day, avoid chasing breakouts and instead wait for pullbacks into rising EMAs.

Avoid taking low-conviction 'fair' trades just to stay active; piling up small losses on marginal setups erodes confidence ('mental capital'), which is worth protecting the same way you protect account equity.

Adapt entry tactics to how the market is currently behaving (e.g., trade the shakeout instead of buying opening-range breakouts once the market has repeatedly shaken out breakout buyers) rather than sticking rigidly to one fixed method, because market microstructure changes over time.
When multiple setups can trigger at the same time, predefine your entry decision before the trigger happens so you can react quickly, and accept that you will still miss some opportunities.

Lower-quality ('fair'/B-C grade) entries need a strongly favorable market environment to work; in choppy/sideways markets their win rate drops sharply, so reserve them for confirmed strong-market conditions.

Prefer buying weakness/pullbacks over chasing strength, even in strong stocks capable of running without a pullback; accept missing some of the biggest moves rather than chase extension from the 9 EMA.
Watch for market leaders breaking down from their key EMAs (9/21) and making lower highs before the general index does — this can be an early warning sign that a broader market top is forming.

After a powerful/parabolic prior move, treat new breakout setups with extra caution even when the chart pattern looks bullish: use smaller size, set tighter stops, follow those stops strictly, and weigh the extended market context rather than judging the pattern in isolation.

Failed breakouts near prior highs (large reversal candles slightly above or below the previous swing high) are the most dangerous and most powerful reversal signals to watch for, especially late in an extended uptrend.

Even when a breakdown looks like it confirms a top, be careful shorting into an extended market — breakdowns can fail and the market can find support again before the real top is in, so don't assume any single reversal is definitively the top.
Be wary of stocks rallying straight up into daily/weekly resistance while their EMAs are still trending lower — that kind of move is a red flag, not a buy signal.
If a stock you're watching (or holding) starts losing the rising 9 or 21 EMA, treat that as a huge red flag — it invalidates the setup.

When the general market/indices are extended, it's much harder to find a tight-risk entry on strength — always time individual entries against the health/extension of the broader market, not just the setup in isolation.

No risk, no reward — don't let fear of stopping out or taking a loss cause you to skip good opportunities; take the trade while price is still holding the key level (the invalidation point hasn't hit yet), and if it fails, accept it and re-evaluate.

Decide whether you'll take a breakout before it actually happens — commit to pressing the buy button immediately at the breakout candle rather than waiting 15-20 seconds to confirm, which lowers reaction time and often means chasing.
It's possible to enter before a key-level bounce is confirmed (before the candle even closes), but expect a meaningfully lower win rate for doing so.

When you have a recurring trading problem (e.g. overtrading, entering too many positions at once), diagnose the actual root cause first — is it mental discomfort with size, poor execution, or FOMO/revenge trading — rather than looking for a generic fix.
If you keep getting stopped out repeatedly, drill down into why: are you entering at the wrong time, is the entry itself not optimal, or are you entering somewhat randomly without a clear plan.

None of your biggest/best trades will come from revenge trading during a difficult, losing period — statistically it's undeniable that the best trades never come from those emotional, revenge-driven stretches.
You can't fully eliminate FOMO or revenge trading, but you can gradually reduce it over time through hard lessons and drawdowns — improvement is incremental, not a single fix.

Accept that overnight/gap risk is part of the game — you can't control whether a position gaps up or down, so embrace the uncertainty rather than dwelling on the downside ('never met a successful pessimist').

Before going full-time on trading: build roughly 2 years of consistent track record spanning different market conditions (uptrend, sideways, downtrend), have trading income that clearly exceeds (ideally 2-3x) your day-job income, and keep a financial cushion of at least 6-12 months of expenses.

If you have to ask other people (or discuss with family/friends) whether you're ready to quit your job and trade full-time, you're not ready — when you truly are ready, you'll know it with certainty rather than being 90% sure.
Avoid buying into strength when the broader market/tape is extended to the upside (e.g., after multiple consecutive gap-up days); wait for a pullback instead of chasing.

Want the sector or market to align with the individual stock before entering — prefers to see the sector ETF pull back into its own rising EMA/unfilled gap before buying a stock within that sector, rather than trading the stock in isolation.

Prefers a stock to close strong into a key intraday level (e.g., a 60-minute candle testing the 9 EMA / trendline) before entering; a weak-looking candle heading into its close is a reason to pass rather than anticipate the bounce.

When there is no real structure to place a stop against (e.g., a fast, gappy first-minute candle), use a fixed percentage stop (roughly 1.5-2.5%) instead of a structural one — accepting a lower win rate — rather than chasing a stock that has already extended too far past its breakout level.

A trading thesis or narrative (e.g., "if X's earnings are bad, money rotates to competitor Y") only matters once it's confirmed by actual market/price action — don't trust logic alone without checking how similar situations have played out historically and how the market is actually reacting.
Lowered average risk per trade from about 0.5% of account (prior year) to about 0.3% this year, and considers that reduction a good decision.

Rarely trims winning positions anymore; prefers to hold full size for at least two to three weeks when a stock is working, and has become progressively more comfortable holding larger positions over time rather than de-risking early.

Rarely moves a stop up to breakeven even after a stock has moved favorably; keeps the stop at the original entry-based level and, if he wants to lock in gains, manually exits rather than mechanically trailing the stop.

Typical position size is around 20-25% of account (rarely above 30%), with per-trade risk still held under ~0.3% by using tight technical stops (often under 1% from entry) rather than by cutting position size.

Avoids initiating shorts when market breadth is improving, even if a specific sector looks locally weak (rolling over from a declining 50 EMA) — breadth strength argues other areas will hold up and absorb any single-sector weakness.

After getting stopped out, deliberately stops trading for the rest of the day ("before I get tilted") rather than continuing to search for another entry — treats tilt risk as a hard stop condition, not just a feeling to push through.

Actively tracks his own condition/mood and will cut back on streaming (and by extension, trading) rather than force it when he's not feeling well or not in the right headspace, even taking planned days off.
Don't buy into a gap-up move; wait for a better entry rather than chase strength at the open.
Prioritize getting the most optimal entry possible over taking many marginal trades — this maximizes usable buying power and preserves mental capital between good trades.
The big money is made by sitting tight in a winning position rather than overtrading it (citing Jesse Livermore).

When you have a solid profit cushion and the stock is in an early-stage uptrend, don't trim the entire position ahead of earnings — keep at least a partial position on, since selling it all risks missing a big continuation run.
Don't panic and exit on an earnings gap-down as long as price is still above your predefined stop — a strong uptrend can gap down 7-10% and still hold above support.
An entry is only worth taking if it offers a tight stop (roughly 2% or less); a wider stop makes the setup not worth it.

Don't copy another trader's rules, style, entries, exits, stock selection, timeframe, or chart settings wholesale — learn selectively from others, test it yourself, and keep only what actually works for your own personality.
Buying a pullback into the 9 EMA on a leading stock offers the tightest possible stop and therefore the best risk/reward in a strong uptrend.
When a stock closes below its 9 EMA after riding it throughout a strong rally, that's a high-probability signal the uptrend is ending or at least needs to pause/go sideways.
Market breadth and the behavior of individual leading stocks are the decisive factor for regime/health assessment, not the index chart itself — the index is just made up of the individual stocks.
The same chart pattern should be traded differently depending on the surrounding market context — an identical setup can be tradeable in a strong tape and untouchable in a weak one.

Using a very tight stop on an explosive opening-range move can cause you to miss the trade entirely if it never pulls back — there's a real tradeoff between tight risk control and catching fast intraday movers.
After a very fast, extended rally, expect a pullback in the coming days or weeks; don't get FOMO or chase — wait for low-risk entries instead.

Avoid shorting a stock or sector into a strong, reclaiming weekly candle after a big rally off the lows — wait for it to reclaim (and then lose) the declining 50 EMA and form a tighter, failed-breakout setup before initiating a short.

The best way to answer your own trading questions is to study the charts yourself — working through your own analysis teaches more (new observations, deeper learning) than simply being handed the answer.
Don't change your process for earnings season — manage entries and active positions the same way regardless of whether a name is reporting earnings.

A structural stop placed just below a rising 9/21 EMA support zone gives a clearly defined, low-cost risk, so a pullback-to-support entry offers favorable risk/reward: small defined loss if wrong, large move if the level holds and price turns back up.

Define risk by stop distance and a fixed risk-per-trade, not by a stock's ADR or beta — position size is derived from the stop distance, so two stocks with very different volatility (e.g. 20% ADR vs 5% ADR) can still carry the same dollar risk.

Prefer spreading size across several smaller positions within the same theme/sector (buying a few small bags of chips instead of one family-size bag) rather than concentrating into a single full-size position, because you don't know in advance which name in the group will actually become the leader — or which one hits its stop.

After a huge, extended uptrend, it's unlikely a stock or sector reverses in a straight line down — even names headed for a real downtrend usually go sideways/base near the highs first, producing failed breakouts or breakdowns to short, rather than falling straight down after a huge move.

In a persistently strong market regime, buying pullbacks into support (9/21 EMA) can be more reliable than waiting for classic tight-range contraction, because strong stocks don't waste time chopping near the lows before resuming higher — adapt entry style to what the current market is actually doing.

To judge whether a sector is gaining strength, scan the whole watchlist/screeners daily and look for several (four-plus) stocks in the same sector or industry acting well together, alongside the sector ETF holding/clustering above its EMAs — breadth across names is more reliable evidence than any single stock's action.

Deeply beaten-down assets that finally find a bottom at a key structural level (e.g. a shakeout back to a prior swing low) can rally very fast off the lows in a 'lockout rally' — watch for confirmation at those key levels rather than assuming continued downside just because a name looks beaten down.

It's very hard to exit a trade exactly at the turning point of a trend — expect to frequently cover a short (or exit a long) only to watch price immediately continue in your original favor; accept this as a normal cost of managing the trade rather than a sign you exited wrong.

When the stop on a setup has to be unusually wide, cut position size so total dollar risk stays in the normal range (here: a ~2% stop, roughly his widest in months, was offset by taking a fraction of normal size to keep risk near ~0.5% of account).

Criteria for a good parabolic reversal (short-into-bounce or long-into-flush) setup: (1) the move should be steep — slope getting sharper on the lower timeframe, (2) the reversal candle should have wide range/high volatility, and (3) it should come with volume expansion.
Uses market orders for the large majority of entries/exits (roughly 90% of the time) and limit orders only occasionally (~10%), rather than defaulting to limit orders.

His largest drawdowns have historically come right after his best runs (cited his 26% December drawdown following a strong stretch), so he makes a deliberate point to get more careful with risk after a good run rather than more aggressive.

When performing well and in sync with the market, it's reasonable to scale up conviction — running more positions (e.g. six to seven instead of two to three) — rather than keeping size static regardless of how the year is going.
To fix overtrading, set a hard daily trade limit; to fix not respecting stops, use hard/mechanical stop orders rather than relying on discretion in the moment.

Names the specific mistakes that caused his worst drawdown: ignoring his own stops, increasing size after consecutive losses, and oversizing in an attempt to make back losses in one trade (revenge trading).

Personal exit rule for consistency: never exit outside of regular trading hours (e.g., won't close an overnight/premarket position on adverse after-hours or foreign-market action) — will wait for the regular session open to manage the trade, even if the counterpart market is moving against him overnight.

Views trading communities and social platforms as generally low-value for real help, since most participants there aren't consistently profitable and are more focused on attention or validation; considers grinding it out largely solo one of his best early-career decisions, and says if you do seek outside help, seek out people with actual multi-year track records.
Deliberately delays / doesn't broadcast entries in real time because he doesn't want viewers copy-trading his exact fills.
Shorting tends to move faster than going long because panic is a more powerful force than greed.

Focus on entries offering asymmetric risk/reward: limited downside represented by a tight stop, entered where the trend is changing, so price should start trending in your favor immediately rather than chopping sideways.
Use EMA stacking and slope (e.g. 9/21/50/150 EMA order and direction) to objectively classify a stock as trending vs. sideways/choppy before deciding whether to trade it.
After a strong gap-up move, wait for a pullback into the 9 or 21 EMA before entering long rather than chasing the initial breakout.
Avoid chasing (FOMO) a setup that already looks good but has run too far without you in it; wait for the next proper opportunity instead.
Cover shorts into weakness/extension and lock in profits; the entry price of your next short in the same name is generally going to be higher (worse) than where you covered.
The more extended the market/sector becomes to the downside, the more you should trim/cover shorts, since a snapback bounce after an extended move tends to be fast and strong.
In choppier, more volatile conditions, trail a winning trend-following position with a wider EMA (e.g. 21 EMA) rather than a tighter one (9 EMA) to avoid getting shaken out prematurely.
You don't need a strong technical reason to take profits into weakness on a short - it's always fine to cover some or all when it feels right, because there will always be another opportunity.
Use small risk per trade, especially early in a trading career, to keep drawdowns manageable while you're still gaining experience from losses.
Deep drawdowns commonly trace back to overtrading, taking poor entries, ignoring your own stop-loss, and oversizing positions - not just bad luck.

Use the price action that follows a stop-out as feedback: if the stopped-out position reverses and gaps back above key levels the next day, the broader thesis/market condition may not be as bad as it looked and re-entry can be considered; if it instead breaks down further, that confirms the weakness.
Specialize in the setup type/side (e.g. shorts only, or a specific pattern) that matches your demonstrated edge rather than trying to trade every opportunity in every direction.

Journal your trades after a drawdown and look for patterns in the mistakes, including non-trading factors (personal life, mood, sleep) that may have contributed, so you can recognize the same warning signs in the future.
Review your good/winning trades, not just losses, to identify what made them work and to rebuild confidence during a drawdown.
Copying another trader's system can work as a starting point, but it isn't sustainable long-term - you eventually need to tweak and adapt the rules to fit your own personality.
Taking a loss/getting stopped out isn't inherently bad - it can be useful information that prompts a shift in bias (e.g. from long to short focus).
Gauge overall market health by watching how a broad list of individual stocks is behaving, rather than relying on a single indicator (like a follow-through day) to call a market bottom or top.
After an ambiguous, volatile session with a sharp bounce, stay open-minded to either direction (continuation lower or a real reversal) rather than committing hard to one bias.

The specific pattern (e.g. tight-range consolidation breakout) matters less than whether it satisfies the underlying requirement of asymmetric risk/reward; keep trading a setup only as long as that requirement still holds, even if the pattern occurs less frequently in the current market.

⭐ A tight, unambiguous stop can be the PRIMARY REASON to take a trade, overriding a mediocre setup. On AMD: 'my reason AMD today will be a good short is plainly because there's a tight stop — so I can manage my risk very easily and I can get a pretty high potential risk/reward.' He takes it despite conceding the entry is extended and therefore lower win rate, because the stop is ~1% and sits at a level (high of day = the 9 EMA) where being wrong is obvious: 'you can easily know you're wrong.'

Win rate decays with distance from the declining EMAs: 'the more extended, the farther away you are from the declining EMAs, the lower your win rate will be.' Extension does not disqualify a trade, but it must be paid for with a correspondingly tighter stop.

⭐ SECTOR selection dominates STOCK selection on the short side: 'my stock selection is not really that important — I just identify the weak sector to short. If you look at all the other semi names, most of them are going down since Thursday, like 99% of them. So it doesn't matter actually which stock I pick.'

Prioritising a short watchlist when several names gap into declining EMAs: prefer names with a clean, sustainable PRIOR trend to break. He rejects PATH as the least interesting precisely because 'in the past few months it's going sideways, no really clean or sustainable trend has formed' — a name with no trend has nothing to fail.

The 60-minute chart is the preferred reference for short entries: 50 EMA curling down, 9 below the 50, 21 also curling down, then short the bounce into the declining EMAs. Best when the 60-min 50 EMA aligns with the daily 9.

Wait for weakness to SHOW at resistance rather than anticipating the reversal: 'sometimes I would anticipate the reversal, but most of the time I wait for it to show the weakness when it rallies into the resistance level. If it continues shooting higher, I won't consider shorting.'

⭐ Entry AGGRESSION is conditioned on recent P&L, not just on the chart: 'I got a huge chunk of profit cushions and positive feedback from my shorts, so I can be a little bit more aggressive on my entries. If I am in a drawdown, if I'm red in a year, I will not be this aggressive — I'll wait for the five-minute breakdown.' Same setup, different entry trigger depending on account state.

He does NOT use stops in extended hours or overnight. If a stock gaps through the stop he simply lets it execute at the open. Rationale: overnight gap risk cannot be eliminated, and 'the probability of getting a gap up or a gap down is pretty similar — they probably even out.'

A pullback short that closes near the low of day buys its own gap cushion: 'that's an advantage of a pullback short — if after entry it rolls over and closes near the low of day, it looks pretty weak, so I kind of have some cushion for a gap up tomorrow.' Managing overnight risk via entry quality rather than via a stop order.

Cover shorts on INDEX extension, not on the individual name's support level. Declines to cover SNDK at a pivot-support zone because SPY/IWM are only 'day one on this reversal' and not even below their 50 EMA; he prefers to cover when the indices are extended to the downside — as he did on 17 Jul when QQQ hit a prior swing low. Accepts the cost: 'I will probably give back some profits.'

⚠ Notably refuses to take a side on sell-into-strength vs sell-into-weakness: 'one of the most debatable rules — they both have a lot of supporters and both have their own merits and disadvantages. You need to find the one that works for you, and sometimes what works for that particular market situation.' A softening of the KB's existing 'sell into strength — it's never wrong' principle.

Choppy conditions; watchlist breadth has flipped bearish — the leading/lagging counts have roughly inverted versus two weeks ago. 'A lot of the stocks are not looking great, especially in the tech universe.' Defensive, energy, financials and biotech look better, but he will not trade them: 'I'm not a fan of trading them, so I'm just going to focus mostly on the tech names.'

Very low conviction on the long side: 'if you look at all the previous leaders — the tech names — most of them have made a move in either late 2024 or this year. I have very little confidence or interest in the long side. Very little.' Still tracks relative-strength names to stay open-minded and avoid tunnel vision.

⚠ Bull-trap warning that he says has caught him repeatedly: relative strength in a WEAKENING tape is a trap. 'Sometimes you get a leader with relative strength, and after the market weakness comes in they have MORE follow-through to the downside. I got tricked by this type of bullish stocks, bullish patterns, bullish charts multiple times when the market breadth is really worsening and the peers are really doing bad.'

How he flipped from neutral to bearish: he graded it as roughly '40% bullish, 60% bearish', then the software/data-centre names that looked strong turned out to be few and still under their 50 or 150 EMA. Decisive test: 'in a really strong bull market, for a really strong bounce, it shouldn't be staying right here — at least I want a bounce into the declining 21 or even the declining 50.' Plus no candidate leader to replace semis as the engine of the AI bull market.

Extended-into-the-downside with huge volume is a danger sign for SHORTS near term, not a green light: semis are 'really extended into the downside having huge volume — that is a really really dangerous sign for the short term.' Symmetrically, a strongest-sector top with 'huge volume, high volatility, white candles' after names like SNDK/MU ran ~2,000% lowers the odds of that sector leading the next leg up.

⭐ Indicator parameters are zones, not lines, and the exact setting does not matter: 'any EMA is not a magic line or something — it's like a zone, it's like a range. Sometimes it overshoots, sometimes it just comes close and finds resistance. I'm using the 21 EMA — what if other people are using the 20? Anyone out there use the 19 EMA? It really doesn't matter.'

'What do you think?' is the wrong question: 'that's not an important question at all — it's irrelevant. What does the MARKET think is the most important, and how can we know that? The price.' He explicitly discounts news, analysts and other traders' claims as inputs.

On an unanswerable hold-or-sell decision (SKHY into earnings) he refuses to give a directional answer and suggests flipping a coin, 'because both holding and selling are right — there is no definite answer.' The decision that does matter: size it against your year — if you're down and the trade is green, locking profit may be right; do not treat earnings as a way to win losses back.
'Do not regret after you have made your decision. You can disagree, you can evaluate your decision a few days or a few weeks later — but do not regret the decision you made at that time.'

Weekend preparation is where the plan gets made, because the market is shut: 'that's really good for making the trading plan for today or this week — doing all the preparations in the weekend where the market isn't open, and you can really analyse the picture, analyse the condition more rationally.'

Position management has no universal answer and is found by iteration: 'it's really a process, and you'll gradually find your own way after trying to sell some or trying to hold more — you will find a balance in between for you. Try first and then evaluate later. But it definitely also depends on the market condition.'

Cross-market read: Ethereum pushed above its 13 EMA (which he treats as his 9 EMA) and some smaller cryptos climbed, but most altcoins still look bad. He is 'getting a little bit worried about the market starting a deep correction or even a bear market' — NVDA looks like a failed breakout rolling over, having topped before QQQ.

Stance unchanged from the 7/22 flip: fully bearish/short. Not many tradable ideas this morning, but 'we're getting a small bounce — which could favor the short side': in a downtrend a bounce is supply, an entry opportunity for shorts, not a reason to cover.

Never size up after a losing streak to make the losses back as fast as possible — that instinct (his own, 2-3 years ago) is the first step of a vicious cycle that ends in a larger drawdown. After yesterday's string of stop-outs he explicitly kept size flat and did not 'keep shorting every bounce regardless of the risk or the market.'

Your original idea can be right and your execution decent and you can still lose: a lot of the time price does not follow your expectations, or knocks you out before going your way (MARA stopping him out and then breaking down). That, not bad analysis, is much of what makes trading difficult.

Intraday-short patience rule learned from yesterday's losses: don't take the FIRST 5-minute reversal at the open — that's how he kept stopping out in the first 15 minutes. Waiting for a later, cleaner reversal (WULF today) caught the strong follow-through with none of the churn.

Rotation read on the bounce day: defensive sectors leading, midcaps leading, tech getting beaten down, many names selling off hard into resistance after the open — a risk-off tape beneath a green-ish index, consistent with staying short.

Leader character change as short timing: SNDK surfed the 50 EMA for the entire uptrend; now it is losing the 50 for the FIRST time and bouncing into the declining 50 — the first such bounce after a long trend is the highest-quality short entry ('shorting yesterday would be the best timing'). Whether it now surfs the 50 DOWN, 'no one knows — we will see.'

This correction may be more destructive than people expect, precisely because the post-liberation-day rally taught everyone that buying every dip prints money. Habits and mindsets formed in a lockout/stage-2 rally (2020-21 analog: Tesla, EV names, speculative garbage later sliced in half) get people smashed when the market deteriorates: 'in a very strong uptrend a lot of mistakes would be forgiven... when the market starts to slow down, you're gonna lose all the money back. Buy the dips — until it doesn't.'

Late-stage crowding marker: before April the heat on SK Hynix wasn't crazy, but on this last leg up retail piled into the semi leader with leverage, margin, even loans — the crowd arrives in the last part of the rally. 'There will be another SK Hynix in the future and we'll see the same thing again' — the ticker changes, the story doesn't.

Bear-market playbook from his own 2022 (+4–8%): drastically reduce trade count; accept that shorts learned in a bull market mostly fail at first (nearly all his 2022 shorts lost); most of the year's return can come from ONE well-trailed trend trade (long BOIL). Survival plus one trend carried the year.

Parabolic-extension exit (from Qullamaggie, on his 2022 BOIL trade): when a position accelerates ~17% above the daily 9 EMA, you don't have to wait for the first close below the daily 9/10 — selling into strength is fine, or downshift and trail the 60-minute 9/10 EMA so the lower timeframe takes you out near the top.

Filter the noise by demanding PROOF: he anchored on Qullamaggie's style because Qullamaggie is a verified example of the strategy working at the highest level, while most strategies online (99%-win-rate MACD/RSI/Bollinger 'secret indicator' videos) come with no proof — just a Patreon link and a discount code.
Verify everything with the market: 'everybody could be wrong, but the market is always right.' Even mentors' rules are hypotheses to test against your own fills, not gospel.

How his signature entry was born: reviewing 2023-24 losers he found breakouts/opening-range-high entries stopping him out and THEN going his direction, with rising frequency. Once you find 5-10-20 examples of the same failure, redesign the entry — wait for the shakeout and buy the intraday pullback / 5-minute range breakout reversal instead of the opening-range high. Takeaway: don't blindly follow the standard entry; let your own losing-trade review re-engineer the trigger.

Knowing vs understanding an entry: the tight-range breakout isn't 'the best buy point' because a book says so — it's best because it strictly limits downside and precedes range expansion (high win rate, 10-20R potential). Once you understand the FUNDAMENTALS (defined risk + win rate + reward), the same logic can justify buying a 21-EMA pullback — breakout vs pullback are opposite tactics built on identical reasons.

Keep asking why about every detail in the market (why did Tesla find resistance THERE?). Most of the time you won't find the answer — but the observations you eventually generate yourself are the most valuable thing you own, 'because that originates from you, not the others,' and what you truly understand works far better than what you copy.

Discretionary vs systematic is a personality fit, not a ranking: he sides with the 'art of trading' and keeps no checklist/rulebook, but a trader with a strong ego, emotional swings, or weak self-discipline may be better served by hard rules. 'There is no one way of trading — which one suits you the best?'

The best lessons are always in the drawdowns, the mistakes, the difficult periods, the market crashes (to a viewer who lost 80% overtrading options) — and living through one mania (this AI run, which 'will definitely fade away one day') is what saves your fortune in the NEXT one, decades later.

Into a pivotal event week (FOMC + mega-cap earnings): the events can't be predicted, so sizing is a self-knowledge question — if a 10% gap against you would trigger revenge trading or panic selling, cut exposure BEFORE the event; if you can genuinely handle the volatility, managing positions as usual is not wrong. He trades the chart, not the news/macro — 'the chart would let me know.'

Aggression is earned, twice over: he can flip from heavily long at Wednesday's open to 6-7 short positions by Thursday only because (1) a triple-digit YTD profit cushion absorbs the risk — 'if I'm not up triple digits right now, probably I'm not opening six or seven short positions in one day' — and (2) he's gotten better at throttling down during losing streaks. Without both, the same flip is just overtrading toward a large drawdown; 'you don't have to trade like this.'

Trading the short side as well as the long keeps you from becoming over-bullish in uptrends/sideways markets and helps you spot weakness earlier. The cost: getting chopped in trendless tape and sometimes turning too bearish during a normal base — but the benefits outweigh the disadvantages.

Aggressive sizing is only an edge when done CORRECTLY — in hindsight the winners look like front-running, but the same behavior failing produces a large drawdown. Reward always comes from risk; the job is maximizing return while actively managing the drawdown — 'and it's not easy. I definitely got lucky this year.' He also says he does not really use volume on lower timeframes (114:29).

When the evening watchlist review shows breakdowns everywhere — leaders rejected at the declining 9, gap-downs across groups, leader count shrinking — close the long book proactively that evening; don't wait for each individual stop to be hit.

The QUALITY of a bounce is information: off a weekly support you want it quick and strong (like crypto 2023); a bounce that hangs around the declining 50 EMA for days is failing, and repeating the pattern of the last failed cycle.

Trying to pick the turning point because you don't want to miss the reversal is paid tuition — repeated stop-outs while price goes nowhere after each stop is the market saying it's chop, not a reversal; the stop-out cluster itself is the signal to stand down.

The better a setup looks on the long side at resistance, the better it is on the short side if it fails: an inside-day 'breakout' right at the anchored VWAP from all-time highs traps breakout buyers whose stops fuel the move down — a classic failed breakout; an overshoot of the AVWAP is the ideal short scenario.
Trade what you see: if the candidate short keeps going higher without showing weakness, don't short it on the way up — wait for the failure.

Beware the laggard's tricky bounce: a name that topped BEFORE the market (made lower highs while the index made higher highs, 9<21<50 with the 50 flattening/turning down) then prints a strong-looking bounce with apparent relative strength — breaking a previous day high, reclaiming EMAs — straight into the supply range of prior red candles. That is a dead-cat bounce / bull trap, not new leadership (LITE now; OPEN January 2026). Don't buy it; when market and sector are below declining EMAs, it's a short candidate.

Judge a suspicious bounce by its FORWARD behavior, not the pattern: if the name holds above its EMAs and makes higher lows while the market makes lower lows, it graduates into a long candidate for when the market improves; if it loses the 9 (or 50) within a day or two on big red candles, the bull trap is confirmed. The pattern label matters less than how it holds up as the market weakens.

In a clear downtrend the method is still the pullback short: shorting bounces gives the highest win rate AND the best risk/reward, and keeps you moving at the same pace as the market rather than chasing breakdowns.

Track the sequential death of speculative groups as a breadth thermometer: quantum gone, nuclear gone, power generators weak, software destroyed, semi laggards breaking — when the speculative money is gone across groups, real damage has been done and a much deeper correction (e.g. QQQ to the weekly 50, ~15%) is on the table.

Range/volatility expansion near the highs on the weekly is a red flag even during an apparently healthy pullback — compare with true leaders (MU, SNDK) whose bases pull back to the weekly 9 QUIETLY, volatility contracting into the next setup rather than expanding.

The checklist to turn bullish again after de-risking: (1) breadth improves — more names showing strength and potential leadership; (2) follow-through appears after breakouts/reversals instead of instant failure; (3) your own long trades start giving positive feedback; and (4) at minimum the index reclaims its declining 9 EMA.

Before shorting a bounce, check where the index AND the sector ETF sit relative to their declining 9 EMA: if they are still extended below it, they will likely keep bouncing into the declining 9/21 and drag your stock up with them (~70-80% of stocks follow market/sector). Short when the index/sector has already bounced back near its declining EMAs, not before.

Shorting every bounce into the declining 9 EMA has the lowest win rate of pullback-short entries — the 9 is the fastest EMA and pullbacks routinely extend to the 21 or even the 50 before rolling over.

Pullback shorts need bear-market context, not just a red week: an intact weekly uptrend making its FIRST pullback into the rising weekly 21 usually finds support and starts another leg; markets rarely slice through all the EMAs without a bounce or sideways attempt first. Shorting that is completely different from shorting a 3-month downtrend where the 50 EMA is under the 150, the declining EMAs are clustered, and breadth is broken.
Do not short immediately after a strong reversal candle — one that opened lower, recovered the whole intraday loss, and closed near the high of day and the prior day's high.

A relatively-strong stock gapping DOWN into rising daily 9/21 support while its sector ETF also opens red improves the odds of the pullback buy — you are buying support with the sector's selling already expressed (e.g. gapping down into the 9/21 on a day SOXX opens lower).

You spot the next leading theme when several names from the same group (five or six, not one or two) show up in the same day's relative-strength scans — especially if they are bouncing on a red market day.

True market leaders top BEFORE the index: QCOM topped in January 2000 while the Nasdaq ran until March. When the real leaders of the move stall, fail to make higher highs, and show relative weakness while the index grinds higher, get cautious on the whole market.

Blow-off tops print extreme dollar volume relative to market cap: QCOM traded ~1/4 of its market cap in one week at the 2000 top (SNDK ~half). Huge weekly volume expansion plus price acceleration after a long uptrend is distribution, not strength.

Watch the volatility signature, not just price: in a healthy base volatility looks like the uptrend's, but consecutive giant alternating red/green weekly candles near highs (volatility expansion) mark the late stage of a move (Motorola 2000).

True trending leaders never close below the weekly 9 EMA on the way up (QCOM never violated it through a ~600%-then-300% run; works with any fast weekly MA). Riding that line keeps you in far longer than feels comfortable — simple, powerful, and very hard to actually follow. The first weekly close below it after a long run (SNDK last week) is the warning.

Market corrections start from an EXTENSION or a FAILED BREAKOUT, almost never from a flat base or sideways range (2007, 2018 trade war, 2024 examples). If neither structure is present, it is too early to call a top.

The market won't crash in a day — a real downtrend shows multiple signs first (leader breakdowns, failed breakouts, volume/volatility expansion). Wait for the danger signs instead of front-running a top call; standing out from the crowd by top-ticking is not smart, and the market can run far beyond what you can imagine.

When neither side offers clear risk/reward — longs not yet confirmed, shorts already extended down into weekly support — trade less and smaller: 'less is more' until the market proves itself, while still probing new positions so you participate if it works.

Stocks increasingly take out the low of day and then rally back to the highs (stop-run shakeouts). If a name gets you out at LOD but falls right back into confluent support (anchored VWAP + daily 9 + clustered lower-timeframe EMAs), treat it as a re-entry candidate rather than a dead trade — but let the market/breakout buyers confirm first.

99% of trading questions have no model answer — different traders reach different, equally profitable answers. Verify claims yourself and build your own conviction; don't adopt another trader's rule without digesting it, and value the thinking process over being right.

Almost nobody does the boring off-hours study (a chart-study prompt to ~27k viewers drew 11 real replies): the repetitive, un-dopaminergic work — studying past charts, learning from mistakes when the market is closed — is itself the edge, because so few put in the time.
Study historical downtrends, not just uptrends: once for shorting skill, once for staying out of bear markets, and once for recognizing where real turning points form at the end of a decline.
History gives ideas but does not directly repeat — don't over-fit past patterns onto today's market; let current individual charts prove the thesis first.
There are thousands of valid ways to trade and no single model answer - find the style that suits your personality, risk appetite, and character, and don't copy someone else's wholesale.
Managing longs and shorts simultaneously can mess with your mind; if it does, it is easier and simpler to focus on one side of the market at a time.
Size shorts exactly like longs: position size is derived purely from stop width and the fixed amount of capital you are willing to risk per trade.
Don't put a timer on study - value the process over the result. How you approach and drill a problem matters more than whether you reach a conclusion this time.
Replay historical periods side by side (e.g. long AMD while short Square in late 2021) to train your eyes on market dynamics and test whether an approach could work for you.
Do your own study to make knowledge yours - you can take ideas from others' sharing, but you have to verify everything yourself; the market leaves puzzles in the charts for you to discover.
After a stretched, high-volume uptrend, a failed breakout at the prior swing high that builds the first lower high marks the end of the uptrend the vast majority of the time (he estimates ~98-99%).
Price respects unfilled gaps quite efficiently - use prior unfilled gaps as support/resistance levels for entries and targets.

Check the sector/theme before the stock: short weak stocks in weak sectors (never a laggard in a strong sector), and go long where many peers in the theme show strength. Then work top-down: theme, weekly, daily, intraday.
Short broken-down leaders on the first bounce or first pullback into the declining 9/50 EMA, ideally where it confluences with prior swing lows and the declining weekly 9.

To time a short intraday, wait for the 5-minute candle to lose momentum, then drop to the 1-minute chart and use the anchored VWAP from the open (or high of day) for the entry - it works beyond parabolic shorts.
Always hunt for entry tactics that tighten the stop - a tighter, logical stop is what maximizes risk/reward per trade (vs e.g. a 2% stop from a 5-minute breakdown).
Candlestick pattern names are gimmicks - the same chart can read bullish (e.g. morning star) in isolation; context of theme, extension, and volume decides the trade, not the pattern.
Cover shorts into weakness rather than trailing all the way down: the faster the flush, the more you cover; if price drifts down slowly and orderly, trail longer.
Cover short positions before the company's earnings rather than holding through the event.

Only take a mean-reversion long after a genuine panic flush - one huge red candle undercutting all support (e.g. into the weekly 21 EMA). If the decline is slow and orderly with no panic, skip it; the base needs more time.
Don't buy a stock showing relative weakness / lagging the market, especially after a quick huge-volume correction from the top of its last push higher.
There is no certainty in markets, only probability - anyone who tells you something is definitely going up or down is a scammer.

After a sector runs hot and a name is already up ~250% in 3 months with peers rolling over, the odds of another 100% leg are low - most of the buying power has been consumed by the run and the late gap-ups.

Your own trade feedback is the best market indicator: in a strong market even bad entries get rewarded, but when even good entries get stopped out - a losing streak of 10-20 - the market has turned unfavorable to your style.

Tight stops raise your trade frequency, which gives you more and timelier feedback from the market - consecutive stop-outs are a useful signal, not just a cost, if you act on them instead of spiraling.

He cut risk per trade from 0.5% to 0.3% (sometimes less) this year to control drawdowns; tight stops still produce solid position sizes, and a higher number of entries compensates for the smaller unit risk.
If you are in a drawdown and don't know what you're doing, stop trading for a while and take a rest.
In a middle-of-the-range market with no clear direction, there is no need to push - and don't get influenced by social-media noise, FOMO, or panic.
Superior returns require luck (a market that cooperates with your style) plus a tight-stop approach that maximizes risk/reward - don't expect top-decile results in a choppy, weak uptrend.
A gap up into declining 9/21 EMAs and prior resistance after a big rally is not healthy action — those levels are where to focus short entries.
A strong Russell/IWM weekly historically lowers the odds of a >15% correction in SPY/QQQ — but treat it as reference only, never as a standalone reason to buy or sell.
Cap same-sector exposure: even if a setup is good, skip it when you already hold multiple positions in that sector on the same side.

The first pullback (long) or first bounce (short) into the 50 EMA after a breakdown/character change is a high-quality entry, especially in a stock that previously respected its moving averages closely.
Be willing to take a few tries at a high-conviction level with tight stops until the stock proves the thesis wrong.
Pre-compute position size before the open: shares = (account risk %, e.g. 3%) / (stop distance %). ~1% stop -> ~3x risk in position value, 1.5% stop -> ~2x; wider than 1.5% -> size down further.
Place the stop order immediately after the entry fills — never sit in a position without a working stop.
Use market orders (not stop-limits) for stop losses so the exit is guaranteed to fill when the stop price is hit.
Overnight gap risk is part of the game and roughly symmetric; a wider stop does not reduce the chance of a close landing near your stop, so don't widen stops to 'avoid' gaps.
Prefer shorting the stock itself over inverse/leveraged ETFs: the ETFs are less liquid, a volatile underlying doesn't need leverage, and every ETF forces you to track a second chart.
You don't have to be net bullish or bearish to be profitable — there is more than one correct play; in a polarized tape being in the right stock matters more than the directional call.
Review charts manually across sectors: the act of filtering hundreds of charts is itself how you read relative strength/weakness and the general market.

Let where the market opens relative to key levels (declining EMAs, unfilled gaps, AVWAP) decide timing: if the open favors your bias, take entries in the first 15-30 minutes; if it opens flat/weak against your bias, wait for the bounce into those levels.

Leverage doesn't change per-trade risk when risk is defined by tight stops; it lets you hold many small-risk positions at once (e.g. >10 at ~25% average size) and finance new trades with open profits when the market is paying.

The weekly/daily chart is the thesis and the lower time frames are only execution — take intraday entries only in the direction that aligns with the higher-time-frame read, and return to the big picture when time frames conflict.

Anchor entries to daily levels (9/21/50 EMA) with all the clues lining up — theme strength/weakness, relative strength, distribution candles (big red bars, long upper wicks) — rather than a single intraday candle pattern; exact intraday trigger can stay discretionary once the daily context is right.
New traders should be more systematic about entry rules — it reduces overtrading and makes it clear whether an entry is solid.
Treat shorts as short swings of a few days (shorter holds than longs) outside of true bear markets — but beware covering into ordinary strength too early.

In choppy markets, mostly sit in cash but keep working: study relative strength across sectors and run imaginary trades (where to enter, whether a scary bounce should stop you) so you don't panic-cover or panic-sell when holding real positions.

Sell longs into strength once they close below the 9 EMA on the 60-minute chart; be quick and lenient on selling rather than waiting for full confirmation (he often exits on the first 60-minute candle instead of the daily close).
Cover shorts into weakness and book the profit rather than holding for a longer trend move.

Use your own trade feedback as a situational-awareness signal: when shorts start working and recently-closed longs keep weakening, treat it as evidence of a change of character or the start of a downtrend.
Weigh individual watchlist stock action more heavily than the index chart: many names cracking the 50 EMA (some the 150 EMA) is bearish even while the index holds its EMAs.

Increasing volatility after an uptrend — wide-range candles, alternating gap-ups and gap-downs, undercut-reclaim-breakout-gap-down sequences — is a sign of momentum loss and a market that needs to rest or roll over.
Don't short into potential support (e.g. the 60-minute 50 EMA); wait for a bounce into the declining 9/21 EMAs for a better risk/reward entry.
The perfect entry may never appear — sometimes you must take an imperfect entry rather than wait forever for the textbook bounce.

The chart pattern is not the reason for the trade: sector weakness, relative weakness versus peers (lower highs while the group makes higher highs), and EMA structure drive the decision — the pattern just happens to look textbook.

A huge-volume range-expansion reversal after an extended rally rarely starts a new uptrend right away; expect chop or a downtrend while the 9/21 EMAs come down and dip-buyers at the 50 EMA are exhausted.
The faster and more parabolic a move gets after a long rally, the higher the probability it is topping; when the strongest leader of a group reverses, it can mark the end of the whole group's move.
With declining breadth after a big rally, prefer missing a potential rally over being aggressive on the long side; don't trust the first bounce until new leadership forms.

Don't flip between longs and shorts rapidly; if the market reclaims its EMAs against your short thesis, sit out rather than immediately hopping to the long side, to avoid getting hammered from both sides in chop.
In choppy, low-conviction conditions keep position risk tiny (e.g. ~0.15% of equity) so a stop-out is only a paper cut.

Judge volume rules through your own study instead of accepting book rules: low-volume breakouts can still lead the strongest rallies, and the deep-dive process (what you look at, what works, what doesn't) matters more than the tools.
Taking real rest matters: it's acceptable to sacrifice some trades and profits for a genuine break instead of grinding continuously.
Let emotions from mistakes pass quickly — focus on the next trade instead of dwelling on missed entries or panic sells.
Treat your recent trade feedback as a market signal: when solid, well-selected setups keep getting stopped out, the market itself is telling you to cut exposure and reassess your posture.
Judge a group by its leader: in a strong uptrend the leader must bounce hard off the 9 EMA. A failed 9 EMA bounce that drifts sideways near the low of day is an early warning to sell the whole group.
Parabolic/climactic dollar-volume after a huge extended run (e.g. consecutive ~$100B volume days after a near-1000% move) often marks the swing high or the end of the uptrend.
When volatility expands after a long rally (big gaps up and down, wide candles, failed breakouts), it generally means distribution or consolidation, not continuation.

Individual names showing relative weakness before the sector breaks (losing the 9/21 EMA, 9 crossing below 21, repeated failed breakouts, first close below the 50 EMA) flag the coming turn and become the pullback-short candidates.
Avoid trading the first 15-30 minutes after open. If the sector ETF gaps down and you want to short, wait for the bounce instead of chasing the open.
Once a breakdown has already extended, it is too late to short. Wait for the rebound into the declining 9/21 EMA (or the anchored VWAP from the swing high) for the short entry.
In a weak group's bounce, short the names that get rejected at the 9 EMA while retesting prior base/swing lows -- a breakdown-and-retest trend-continuation setup.
Skip groups that are acting well but moving too slowly -- only trade the fast movers.
Scale out by selling into strength rather than dumping the entire position at once into weakness.
When the action feels weird, strange, or uncomfortable midday, act on it -- take positions off rather than staying stubborn or long-biased.
Losses are a chain reaction: early sloppy losses consume your risk budget and force you to pass on the day's best setup later. Protecting the open preserves capacity for the A+ trade.
Do not get aggressively bearish inside a potential chop zone. Require confirmation -- e.g. the index closing below the 9 and 21 EMA -- before increasing short exposure.
Use holidays and long weekends to digest the action across names, review your trades, and fix mistakes so you come back with a refreshed mind.
