He is often early on both long and short ideas; a directional feel can take days or weeks to play out, and the market can push higher before reversing. On the weekly he wants to see an overshoot of the prior candle high then a reversal.

Be willing to be over-selective and sit out: avoid trades (e.g. oil) where the risk/reward isn't attractive, especially when a new position would conflict with existing exposure and risk irrational panic decisions.
Sit out the first 15-30 minutes of the session; entering in the opening window has a low win rate, especially around earnings gaps.
Taking many small losses chewing up buying power compounds the damage; a stream of unexpected stops drains both capital and the ability to size the trade you actually want.
Selling a winner to fund a new idea usually backfires: the original works while the new one stops you out, and the regret of that is worse than the regret of missing a fresh opportunity.
He likes basing setups where the EMAs are tightly clustered and starting to cross up (e.g. 9 crossing 21/50); buy the weakness as things line up.
To enter an extended short candidate he wants acceleration to the downside: a huge red candle (5-min down 5-10%+) with increased volume engulfing the prior small candle.
When a stock halts repeatedly you cannot manage risk (can't place stops or get filled between halts); such names may not be worth trading no matter how attractive.
Holding winners is a major improvement: he held a 7-week position without selling a share, resisting the old habit of selling the moment a leader looks like it will lose the 9 EMA.
Prefer dollar volume over share volume because it shows how much money is actually trading the name; two stocks with similar share volume can differ by orders of magnitude in dollar volume.

Climax tops in commodities (gold/silver after a multi-year run, with a ~10% one-day reversal on a 3% ATR) have a high chance of not going higher and rhyming with prior parabolic-then-multi-year-decline patterns. History doesn't repeat but it rhymes.

Surviving a difficult market and staying focused even when it's bad is what positions you to capture the fast easy-money move that follows; those who quit or stopped watching miss the straight-up rally.
Trade the strongest name in the hottest sector; sector/relative strength matters more than the chart pattern itself.
A stock with extreme volume on a parabolic run is likely seeing institutions building shorts; even leaders may need a longer base/deeper pullback (to the 50 or weekly 21 EMA) after a huge move.

When you start doubting your entry and feel low conviction, that often means the trade 'is getting there' (near a top/turning point); if you can't get the parabolic volume signal you want, it's okay to skip the trade.

For a parabolic short he wants a huge dollar-volume blow-off candle on a lower time frame (e.g. 5-min >100M dollar volume, or a 300M+ candle that closes below the 9 EMA) before entering; size is naturally tiny when the spread is wide.
Getting filled with a small size on a wild parabolic was lucky: a 20-25% position would have been brutal; small size on extreme-volatility names protects you when stops can't get through.
Never go long a euphoric parabolic just because it might run further - when you get the urge to chase the top, do the opposite or don't trade it; you'll get destroyed on the second or third attempt.
Plan profit targets in advance for a short: first target the hourly 50 EMA, then the daily 9 EMA (ideally undercut a bit) before considering more.

Markets revert to ~8-10% annual returns long term but go through short-term variance: a 20% up move can be followed by a 20% down move; we haven't had a >50% correction in ~20 years and one will eventually come.
Protecting mental capital is the priority: after building a good portfolio with no losing trades for days, avoid over-trading and paper cuts that would worsen decision-making in the coming pullback.

When the index is extended and far from the 9 EMA, lean back and wait; you must stay away from new longs until the market pulls back and the EMAs catch up. After a straight-up move, expect ~1-2 weeks before better pivots form.
Setup-selection priority: prefer the hottest sector first (even a worse chart in a better sector), then the faster-moving / higher-ADR name, then the higher-dollar-volume / more liquid one.
Hold original winners rather than selling them to chase new ideas; don't let new ideas influence decisions on existing positions (a mistake he made a lot in 2024).

Favor breakouts from a long base over a short one - the long-base breakout is generally the most powerful; also prefer liquid (>~300M total volume) and higher-priced names over sub-$3 stocks with wide spreads/high commissions.

Risk sizing scales with stop tightness, not a fixed dollar risk: as he tightened stops over the years he could put on a 25% position at 0.5% risk; he reduced risk from ~1-2% to ~0.5% as the account grew and trade count rose (~100 trades/month).

His chronic mistake is selling winners too early (cites SMCI: sold and it ran another 100% in 3-4 weeks). He aims to be more lenient on selling than on entries - trim ~15% into strength and hold the rest via the 9 EMA for 5+ weeks.

When a position opens right at your stop, it can be worth waiting the first 30 minutes to see if it reclaims the EMAs rather than eating an immediate first-minute shakeout - accepting up to ~2.5x the original risk as a deliberate discretionary call.
Don't impose a hard limit on re-entering a stock: as long as the market hasn't fundamentally flipped and you manage risk, re-entry is fine.
After a huge gap up / V-shape recovery, a pullback to the 9 EMA is essentially guaranteed; don't chase the gap - be patient and buy the pullback, or you'll get shaken out.

Avoid shorting a stock in a strong weekly uptrend (50 EMA far below 21) and in the strongest sector (semis); an undercut-and-reclaim of the 9 EMA is poor short timing - wait for a fakeout/rejection above the 21 EMA, and demand a quick reversal away from the level.

Whether to add or book profits depends on entry cushion, current position size (don't over-concentrate >~30% in one name), and overall exposure/margin. Don't sell on the gap-up earnings day itself if you already have a cushion - you'd only be giving back profit, not capital.
When mediocre-watchlist names upgrade to the leading watchlist, market breadth is improving and you should tilt focus to the long side.
On a strong position trade, follow the 9 EMA on the weekly chart to avoid getting shaken out of huge runners.
Reduce position size for less-liquid, lower-priced, wide-spread small/micro-cap names.
Just after a correction is the best time for position trading because the odds of a prolonged uptrend are higher; aim to hold winners longer with larger size.
Trade ~90% on technicals and ~10% on themes/industry; you don't need to read financials, you just need to know what the stock keeps doing.
Once a leading runner is ~10% extended above the 9 EMA it is too fast to chase; the last leg up in stage two is the fastest and craziest.
Don't chase on a huge gap-up day for longs, and don't short into a gap-down day; gap days are poor entry timing for the corresponding side.
Ignore news, CNBC, FT, Trump's Twitter; only the charts matter and news that is pre-announced is mostly already priced in (especially the bad side).
A ~1% tight stop (~0.3% of account) lets you take many attempts cheaply; even if stopped out it's no big deal, and if it works the risk/reward is huge.
In the current regime, pullbacks with tight stops work better than breakouts because breakouts no longer offer tight stops; find the entry tactic that gives the tightest possible stop right now.

For a new uptrend, price must first hold above the fastest (9) EMA; pulling back to a rising 9 EMA and finding support confirms it, and on lower time frames support must hold before higher time frames.
For shorts, selling into strength is welcome anytime; this also makes it easier to hold and avoid being shaken out.
Keep rules and setups as simple as possible; complex multi-rule checklists make decision-making too hard.
Don't set stops too tight out of greed; placing a stop below the 5-minute candle low can avoid getting shaken out of a good entry.
A push to new highs followed by a failed breakout is one of the most common tell-tale signs of a double/climax top, especially with a climax top on the left.
On a pullback day into the 9 EMA, take more attempts on the long side when the leaders are doing well; this is good timing for pullback buys.
For shorts, selling into weakness is welcome anytime; if you already sold some into strength you can hold the rest longer for a close below the 9 EMA.
Sizing below 3% per trade is optional and situational; deepen the drawdown (e.g. past ~10%) before cutting risk further.
It's hard to short an uptrend; avoid being aggressive or large on the short side while price keeps gapping higher.
Watch quietly-setting-up groups nobody is bullish on (e.g. crypto when everyone talks oil/inflation/war); a shakeout-and-reclaim that closes back above the 9/21 EMA is a strong sign of strength.
After leaders close above the EMAs, get in within the first few days of the new uptrend; they tend to snap up so fast you won't get a later entry.
Keep risk per trade under ~1% (often 0.3-0.5%) so even a gap-down that doubles or triples your intended loss stays manageable (~1-1.5%).

Trade liquid stocks (above ~50M daily dollar volume); they shake out less, move cleaner, and have better odds of becoming true leaders. Avoid focusing on small/micro caps unless you have a special edge.

Selling some into strength is never wrong and can give you confidence to hold a larger position through later pullbacks without being shaken out; but early in a new uptrend favor holding for a longer move.
Once in a trade, accept the outcome and move on; the more you try to control the outcome, the harder trading becomes.
Let your own positions tell you the regime: when existing longs (e.g. Dell, Marvell) build higher lows during a correction, that positive feedback signals the long side has potential.
Trade what you see, not what you think: get more bullish only when your longs work and the market holds the rising 9 EMA; don't be aggressive long once it loses the 9 EMA.

After two gap-down days, a gap-up back above the hourly 9 EMA (extended from the daily 9) is good timing to try some bounce/mean-reversion longs, but it's fine to sit out while the market is still below the 9 EMA.
Shorting during a downtrend builds a profit cushion before the next uptrend, so a failed bounce-long only costs cushion, not capital.
Never widen a stop or take high risk to chase; only in rare cases (2-3 times/year) use an intraday entry to chase a name you really want in a great market.
In a drawdown, sizing up to win it back creates a death spiral; instead reduce size or sit out, because drawdowns mean either you're trading badly or the market doesn't suit your style.
Prefer liquid stocks breaking out from long bases over names just riding the 50 EMA straight up; the most powerful moves come from real bases.

Bad market conditions are the best time to review and correct your mistakes (entries, sizing, stops, stock picking) by reflecting on losing trades; a good market will always come, so protect your mental and financial capital until it does.
No panic yet: with the VIX still under 30 and money still flowing into the strongest small/micro-cap leaders, sentiment isn't bearish enough; wait for a huge flush that stops out even the leaders.
When breadth is low and leadership is shrinking, stop hunting breakouts and longs; this kind of market punishes traders who chase every breakout.
A genuine support reaction is a fast V-shaped bounce reclaiming the 9 EMA quickly; a slow, weak bounce off the EMA (no quick reclaim) is a warning, not a buy.
You don't need to trade every day or master every setup/side/condition; you can avoid the shorts you dislike and still make a good return.
Use the oil top as a tell for a market low: the market likely finds at least a short-term bottom when oil tops; watch ~120 prior high and ~105 as levels.
Don't trade extended names long: a stock 50% above its 50 EMA and nowhere near the daily 9 EMA is a poor spot to take a long despite a shallow pullback.
On parabolic-top shorts, cover when price closes back above the 9 EMA; a close above the 9 is the signal the downtrend is failing.
Sell into intraday strength, especially in a weak market with little follow-through; willing to lock profits on longs into gap-up strength near prior highs.
For reversal shorts, the highest-risk-reward entry is the bounce into the declining 9 EMA after price has closed below it and the 9 has started to decline.

When more leaders close below the 9/21/50-day and the market stays range-bound, treat breadth as deteriorating and lean to the short side; the general market is the single most important breakout filter.

Tightening stops to under 2-3% (~0.35% account risk) lets you size larger into winners and tolerate frequent stop-outs; performance lifted off after tightening stops. Size down on ADRs, small/micro caps, and high gap-risk names.
Copy other traders early, but eventually discard most of it and build your own style around the edge only you possess; know yourself.

Maintain three daily watchlists by simple daily-chart rules: leading (price > 50 EMA and 50 EMA > 150 EMA), lagging (the inverse), mediocre (in between). Keep rules minimal so you can flip charts fast and stay rational doing scans after the close.
Don't over-trade the first 15 minutes; getting too aggressive at the open led to being shaken out three times. Be patient before committing.
Choppy, range-bound conditions are a good training market: if you can survive or profit here, you'll capture big gains once the market improves.

On parabolic-top shorts, the highest-risk-reward entry is the bounce into the declining 9 EMA after the first close below it; build conviction by studying historical parabolic tops (e.g. 1980 gold) that rhyme with the current chart.
When shorting and the market rips against you, recover/cover shorts rather than panic-sell longs; trimming into strength to lock profits while keeping the core is the disciplined move.
Pick a small set of favorite moving averages and stick to them; using too many MAs over-complicates decision-making, and you must accept missing trades your chosen MAs don't capture.
A tight ~1% stop makes a stop-out cheap while the upside-if-right is huge, so a good risk-reward play is worth taking even if it fails.
Judge a trade by the quality of your decision-making, not the outcome; if the entry and process are solid, you can be happy to take the loss when stopped out.
Pick one side and stay on it as long as possible in a choppy market; constantly flipping between longs and shorts (as in last December) can easily kill performance.
Treat a clean gap-up above all EMAs, prior highs, resistance, and AVWAP as an EP and enter; but a stock that opens flat/down and only rises 5% after the open is too late to chase.
Avoid opening-range-breakout entries on EPs now (too many fakeouts); wait for the intraday 5-min or 15-min candle breakout instead. On too-wide stocks use the 5-min breakout, not the 15-min.
When closing a long into a gap-up you can be casual/aggressive about the exact level, but to build a new short position wait for it to reach resistance more precisely.
Don't short a one-day bounce into declining EMAs as a rule; normally wait 2-3 days, since quick one-day reversals back below the EMAs are rare.

Plan trades days ahead, before the chart fully confirms; you should be five steps ahead and not improvise after the open. This keeps you focused on the best ideas and immune to news and other people's noise.

Trade a sector ETF rather than an individual stock when expressing a sector view; a single name (e.g. AMD) can bounce, fake your stop, and reverse, so the ETF separates the thesis from single-stock noise.
Demand a high-standard entry right at resistance, not somewhere already extended; a poor-location entry risks a gap-through-stop and a larger-than-planned loss.
Simply bouncing into the declining 9 EMA is a low-win-rate short entry; one try is fine, but taking two or three losses on it is unwise (overtrading).
Stay focused on the short side in this pocket; don't get distracted by the strong leaders, watch the laggards, the weakness, and the declining breadth.
Scale out partials (~25%) into weakness/target areas rather than all at once, and don't celebrate early until the short is actually closed.
Risking ~0.3% per trade means you'd need 10 stop-outs in a row to hit a 3% daily drawdown, which rarely happens unless you overtrade or get chopped on both sides the same day.
Use ~3% as a mental daily-drawdown stop, but count only new trades taken that day (not unrealized losses on existing positions); focus on drawdown from peak equity or over the week, not a single day.
Don't trust any move and don't chase: before a strong close back above the EMAs, look only for the short side, especially in the Nasdaq with EMAs trending down and weekly below the 9/21.
The best risk-reward short is taken where the EMAs cluster close together; shorting after price loses the daily 50 / weekly 9 and the EMAs cross down is more optimal than shorting a simple bounce.

Trade one side at a time; flipping between longs and shorts in a choppy market gets you chopped up and can produce big losing streaks (last December's 26% drawdown came from repeatedly switching directions).
Prefer the weaker name within a strong sector for a sympathy short (e.g. CK/Western Digital over the leaders), and use leaders' 9 EMA and swing-high AVWAP as the resistance reference.
Very tight stops (risking <0.3% per trade) let you take many positions without fear of a big drawdown even if a bounce stops you out of most of them.
In an indecisive market, prepare for both sides and ignore the indices for a bit; don't trust any move, wait for a stock to pick a direction before committing.

Shorting gap-ups into declining EMAs or swing-high AVWAP has been working well; for an aggressive reversal short you must time the bounce into the declining 9 EMA precisely and act on the first opportunity, not wait for the next day.

A cleaner short is to wait for price to lose the weekly 9 / daily 50 EMA first, let the EMAs cross below, then short the pullback; the most reliable short is when price consolidates under all the EMAs with the EMAs clustered close together.
Always be prepared for the trade to be over; stay ready to flip with the reversal if one appears.
Avoid entering a short too close to an earnings report (e.g. Circle reporting Wednesday) — it's too risky.
In a chop-chop market, lean on the power of sitting out; the edge is situational awareness, emotional management, and avoiding over-trading/FOMO rather than forcing entries.
When short against an uptrend, move the stop to break-even faster than normal because shorting a stock in an uptrend is dangerous; this limits damage to the equity curve across repeated stop-outs.
Don't increase size during a losing streak; if anything reduce size. Trading smaller is the main lever for limiting drawdown.
Stack confluence: short when the index (QQQ) is at a resistance level AND the individual stock is also at resistance, to increase the odds the trade works.
After a strong/extended day, wait for one to two more days of consolidation above the EMAs (ideally near the 21 EMA) before entering rather than chasing.
Don't let the index defining a top happen in your head too early; being habitually too early on shorts costs money, so hold back and be more patient.
Sitting out is a valid and good outcome; deliberately reduce the number of trades per year and treat no-trade days as practicing the sit-out skill.
Be skeptical of buying breakouts after a long, stretched uptrend with no decent base and narrow breadth; a pullback to the 21 or 50 EMA is healthier for sustaining an uptrend.
Wait for the market to confirm weakness before shorting into a choppy tape; don't pre-empt the move and risk getting chopped up.
Intraday/breakout-candle stops give tighter risk but a lower success rate; sitting the stop at the low of day is wider but more reliable — it's a tradeoff to weigh per setup.
In a market with only 2-3 day follow-through on either side, take short swings and sell into strength / cover into weakness after a couple days rather than holding for a big move.
Keep a holistic feel for both sides of the market; don't tunnel-vision only on weakness (shorts) and ignore stocks showing strength.
Risk only ~0.3% of the account per trade; reducing per-trade risk makes losing streaks and drawdowns far more manageable and suits an aggressive lower-timeframe entry style.
Wait for the close to confirm strength before acting; a strong first 30-60 minutes isn't enough — names rallying into resistance must prove they close strong, not just spike.
Skip the first 15 minutes after the open — it's super volatile (a name can be +10% then -5%); sit out and observe before entering.
No need to rush entries in a choppy market; if it holds above the EMAs and doesn't quickly reverse, then start searching for longs or get more aggressive.
For a short to confirm a resistance, require the stock to close below the 9 EMA for at least two to three days, not a single day.
This market is genuinely difficult; if you're not trading well right now that's completely okay — protect mental capital alongside financial capital.
Favor buying breakouts of multi-month bases and trading pullbacks to the 9/21/50 EMA over chasing extended names; the first retest of the 9 EMA is often the best entry.
Don't try to eliminate emotions — acknowledge them but don't let them drive decisions; euphoria leads to chasing, drawdowns lead to widening stops or revenge-risk.
Most retail can't beat the index after hundreds of hours of study; the honest advice for non-serious traders is to buy QQQ/VOO and hold for 10 years.

For parabolic shorts, study topping patterns: after a parabolic top a stock usually builds a lower high before the downtrend, and trendlines getting steeper (60-70 degree slope) signal the top is near.
Holding shorts over a long weekend carries gap risk you can't hedge; size down or avoid adding before holidays since you can't exit on a Monday gap.
A long, exhausting chop market (longest since 2020) is the best training ground — surviving or profiting here makes the next trending market feel easy.
After a big drawdown/losing streak, stop trading for 2-3 days to refresh and rebuild confidence, then restart with small size; build patience incrementally from each painful drawdown.

Move the stop to break-even the next day once the 9 EMA crosses above the entry; but if the stock is choppy or the market is pulling into a key support, leave the stop in place to avoid being shaken out before a bounce.
Avoid opening-range-high breakouts, especially the first 15 minutes (volatile, wide spreads since ~2023); reduce frequency and wait for pullbacks into declining EMAs on a gap up.
Shorting a 9 EMA pullback alone has a low success rate — you must short at resistance, with the market environment cooperating; market condition matters more than how good the chart looks.
Take profit more aggressively on shorts than longs (cover into weakness); on longs follow the stop and don't cover prematurely.

Categorize watchlists by EMA structure (leading: 9>21>50, 50>150; lagging: the exact inverse; mediocre in between) but treat the rules as flexible conventions, not fixed laws — adapt to your own personality and preferences.
Don't cut a working short too early just because of exposure or relative strength; covering before the stop is hit can forfeit large follow-through (PLTR cost him ~13% more downside).
Best short entries are pullbacks that fill a post-earnings gap into the daily 9 EMA + anchor VWAP, or rejections of the declining 9/21 EMA at the anchor VWAP from the all-time high.
For aggressive shorts, sell into strength to scale out; you don't need to trail every short to the bottom — keep a 'smile'/runner position while booking the meat of the move.
When the pre-market scan shows most names in downtrends and only defensive (staples) names up, the breadth is bad — favor the short side and don't chase extended names higher.
If anticipating a breakdown (aggressive early entry before confirmation), take less risk — use only a fraction (e.g. half) of your normal per-trade risk.
A 50% QQQ run with every dip bought and snap-back rallies can't last forever; recall the market's long-run average is only ~8-10% annually before assuming endless upside.

Trade with very tight stops (mostly under 2.5%, rarely over 3%) and a low win rate; tightening a stop from 3% to 1.5% can compensate for ~8 losing trades on a 25% return trade and 20-25R on bigger winners.
Risk a fixed ~0.5% of portfolio per trade on average; risk less when trades aren't working, more (6-7%... i.e. larger size at fixed stop) only with high conviction or a profit cushion.
Stop width drives position size: position size = (account risk) / (stop %). A 1.5% stop yields ~20% size, a 1-1.2% stop yields ~25-30%; do the quick math on every trade.
Don't cap total margin/exposure explicitly; instead cap risk-per-trade, and let exposure (up to ~280% long) build naturally only as existing positions work and you derisk them.

Always define and place the stop BEFORE entering (even when bending other rules) so every loss is known and controllable; put it at the low of day for highest win rate, or at the entry/breakout candle low to tighten.
Favor pullback buys over breakouts in markets that reward them: pullbacks give earlier, lower-risk, tighter-stop entries at non-extended support, improving average price and risk/reward.

The best pullback entry is the first pullback to support within a base that has higher lows, ideally at confluence where anchored VWAP + 9/21/50/150 EMA + prior swing high stack; avoid pullbacks 'in the middle of nowhere' or far extended from the 9/21 EMA.

Use anchored VWAP (learned from Brian Shannon) as a key support/resistance on daily, hourly, and intraday; anchor to swing highs/lows or big gap/volume bars, and adjust the anchor to the bar price respects most - it's an art, what matters is the price reacting.
Don't chase: skip an entry if price is more than ~3% above the low of day / ideal entry point.
Intraday trigger is the breakout of the previous bar high after a fast flush to support; use 1-minute candles in the first ~15 min, then 5-minute candles after.
Prefer a sharp V-shaped intraday recovery (buyers stepping in immediately) over a slow gradual late-day recovery; the faster the rebound, the stronger the stock.

Use the weekly chart to clarify the big picture: a daily that looks ugly can be a constructive base if weekly 9>21 and price respects anchored VWAP - don't short or abandon names that are fine on the weekly.
No strict sell rule; scale out ~15-20% into strength when extended on a lower time frame (especially the 1-hour), and close remainder on first close below the 9 EMA.
Bias toward controlling downside over maximizing upside - he sells winners early when skeptical because his weakness is overtrading/extended entries, not leaving gains on the table.
Take profits on shorts faster than longs (within ~2-3 days, into strength/weakness): mathematically a short's edge decays as price falls (a further -50% is only +75% vs +125% staying long).
Focus only on the fastest-moving, highest-ADR names within a hot theme; combined with tight stops this maximizes return potential and risk/reward.

Let the market dictate the setup: trade more pullbacks/breakouts/EPs/parabolics depending on what the current environment rewards; the tight-stop low-win-rate style stays constant, the entry tactic adapts.
Size in percentage terms and grow position size as the account grows - thinking in absolute dollars (not %) keeps many traders from compounding (learned from Qullamaggie).

Build situational awareness from three inputs: your own trade feedback (are new positions working), the indices (QQQ & IWM daily), and your watch-list flow (names migrating to leading vs lagging lists).
Be most aggressive buying during index pullbacks to rising EMAs, not when indices are extended; when breadth is declining, trade less rather than forcing shorts.
Choppy/sideways markets (e.g. his December) punish tight-stop traders via flip-flopping longs/shorts and false signals; the fix is to sit out and trade less, not to keep trying to make losses back.
Beware behavioral slippage: after a losing streak or a missed leader you take random/revenge trades, which compounds the drawdown and bleeds into future decisions (missed the SNDK breakout this way).
It's okay to miss leaders and get stopped out - you can still have a great year; don't feel discouraged or chase what left without you.
When unsure whether to take a setup or sell, ask 'what would a great trader do?' - it eliminates ~90% of random/revenge trades; treat trading as a real business.
Copy mentors early, but as you gain experience adapt the system to your own personality and style (e.g. he progressively tightened stops from 5-7% to under 2.5% because it suited him).
First 13-15 minutes after the open are hard to trade: spreads are wider and most early moves are fakeouts; the real move usually comes 30-60 minutes after the open.
Overtrading drains both financial and mental capital; the gains you miss while recovering confidence after a string of stop-outs also count as a cost of overtrading.
Shift focus to the short side when the general market weakens and breadth deteriorates, but short rebounds into declining EMAs (e.g., declining 9/21) rather than chasing breakdowns.
Cover shorts into weakness/acceleration (gap-down candles) rather than into strength; size up gradually only after building a profit cushion from existing winners.
Only risk more than your normal per-trade amount (>0.5%) when conviction is genuinely exceptional, such as a true once-in-a-decade parabolic setup with a very tight stop.

Market environment contributes more than half of a trade's success; a great-looking chart pattern is not the major factor — your own recent trade feedback (e.g., 8 of last 10 failing) is a more accurate signal than any indicator that it's time to stop pushing.
Don't be too emotional about gains or losses; the emotional intensity of both winning and losing diminishes with experience, and a little detachment is optimal.

On a broad gap-down day into rising EMAs/support levels, prefer buying pullbacks and reversals (e.g., indices pulling into 21/50 EMA) rather than chasing; if market is weak, reduce positions and wait for the next rebound.
Even if bearish, don't short into a fresh gap down — the risk/reward is poor; wait for a rebound into the declining EMAs to short.
Reduce risk per trade to ~0.3-0.4% (down from 0.5%) because trading very frequently raises the odds of losing streaks; smaller risk preserves mental capital and curbs revenge trading.
Trimming too early reduces losses on bad trades but also significantly cuts returns on the good ones; he normally trims after a position is up 3-5R.
Practice progressive exposure by number of trades: start with 1-2 new positions from cash, add to 4-5 only if trades gain traction; cut risk when trades aren't working.
Study your losing trades, not just journal them — look for recurring weaknesses (e.g., raising risk during losing streaks) and fix them.
Obey your stop and ignore the impulsive inner voice; most emotion-driven mistakes (FOMO entries, cutting winners early) come from desire for money — be systematic and forget the money.
Theme is the only fundamental that matters to him; he reads charts only (no financials/ratios) but respects that many profitable styles exist.
A healthy bull market shows rotation — strength broadening to sectors outside tech, not only tech up while everything else is down.
Skip gap-ups where the right side of the base is too short; prefer a longer right side that digests selling pressure before the move, even if it means missing the trade.

Extended breakouts (price stretched from the 9 EMA) have a high failure rate unless the market is super strong; if you take one, use a smaller size or smaller risk to compensate for the low win rate, only when the stop can be kept tight.

Prefer buying pullbacks above the 9/21 EMA (e.g., on the hourly) over chasing; pullback entries are low-win-rate and need a strong market to work well, so be careful not to overtrade them in a weak tape.
Don't take shorts on a parabolic commodity until it closes below the 9 EMA — the 9 EMA is the crucial trigger level for the reversal.
Trade less and stay in one lane — skip 50/50 setups, and avoid doing longs here and shorts there; focus.
Index pullbacks (e.g., Qs to the 50 EMA) are healthy and good for long setups, letting EMAs catch up to names that have run straight up; no need to be too bearish while IWM remains strong.
IWM outperforming the Qs is bullish for longs; since 2008 every market drawdown >15% has begun with IWM lagging the Qs, so IWM being the stronger one makes him more optimistic on a pullback.
Don't take shorts while the indices are still above their EMAs, especially when IWM is much stronger — a stated goal to trade less means skipping those shorts.

Every higher-timeframe uptrend begins as an uptrend on a lower timeframe; for pullback buys, the 5-minute breakout (stop at low of day / breakout candle) is a solid entry timeframe to express the reversal.
Risk only ~0.3% per trade this year (down from 0.5%); when the stop is very tight (~1%) the position size ends up similar anyway, so tighter risk doesn't shrink exposure much.
Prefer to let the 9 EMA catch up before buying a name with a steep left side and little consolidation; an inside day forming today makes tomorrow's breakout ideal.
On extended commodity/parabolic names that have run 60-70%+, expect at least a short-term top; don't keep buying — wait for the reaction at declining EMAs.
Overtrading and random trades are the core failure mode: of 74 December trades only 9 won, ~46% were avoidable 'C' trades taken with no edge — cutting random trades is the main lever for improvement.
Don't switch to longs just because your shorts got stopped out (or vice versa) to chase performance — that mindset is devastating and drives overtrading.
Reduce risk per trade for a high-frequency trader (toward 0.3-0.4%): keep a mentally comfortable max single-day loss (~2%), so at 0.5% risk you can absorb ~4 losses in a row before discomfort.
Position size = (account x risk%) / stop%. Tight stops let you take larger share size for the same dollar risk.
Cap drawdown as an explicit goal; a 26% December drawdown (vs a 20% target) is unacceptable even inside a +969% year — process matters more than the headline return.
Don't over-weight small/micro caps when judging overall market strength; many are doomed-to-zero junk and obsessing over them in December made him too bearish and fed overtrading.
On shorts that work for only a day or two, take profit more aggressively; several December shorts (Q, QBTS) reversed because he wasn't at the screen and didn't bank gains.

Classify the watchlist by EMA strength: leading = price above 50 and 50 above 150; lagging = price under 50 and 50 under 150; everything between is mediocre — but override to 'lagging' any name you consider bearish.

When indices try to climb but the tech-related names (SMH/XLK) are under the 9 and closing below the 21 with the 21 crossing under the 50, those names face pressure climbing into declining MAs — a non-bullish backdrop.

Gap-down risk is a core, unavoidable part of trading; for small/micro caps (<~$2B) a >30% gap down is common, so use smaller size, take profits more aggressively, or avoid those trappy names entirely.

When the 9 is under the 21 (downtrend), a bounce back to the 21 EMA has a very high win rate for shorts; a multi-day base/flag bounce before rejection has a higher win rate than a one-day bounce, though both are tradeable.

Study setups in hindsight across hundreds of examples (he uses the 1-hour chart) to learn which entry context — opening-range, prior-bar breakout, 21 EMA pullback — actually stands out, rather than only chasing rare perfect 5-star setups.
Tight stops are his style and carry their own edge; an 8% prior-day-high stop is not for him — develop a personal style, but risk management is non-negotiable.
In a divergent/weak market, protect profits more aggressively and sell into strength; in a stronger market allow positions more room to pull back.

Don't short after everything has already gone straight down and you have no profit cushion; missing those entries can be a blessing, and don't trade both longs and shorts at once if it doesn't suit you.
Prefer buying the breakout AFTER a pullback rather than the dip itself, because at the rising EMAs you don't yet know if support holds; a breakout-of-pullback gives a defined, easier-to-manage stop.

Wait for the right side of the base to consolidate the selling pressure of the left side; a small/sharp pullback right side isn't ready, and straight-up-from-here off a too-small base is a lower-probability breakout.

When the market has no direction (up one day, down the next) and new long positions aren't working, reduce activity, cut new-position win-rate exposure, and consider that the short side or cash may be the easier play.
In a polarized market you must be excellent at stock selection; be open-minded and prepared for the worst case even when pre-market scans lean you long, and react quickly when things turn.
Cut losses quickly, don't become a bag holder, and never average down.
If you can't watch the close to enforce a 'first close below the 9 EMA' stop, exit early rather than risk a larger overnight drawdown when the market is weak.
Staying in cash is itself a position; don't be aggressive on the short side without cushion, but lean short if the QQQ stays under the 9 EMA.

Risk management is the one constant of trading: always define and cap your risk before entering, know how much you'll lose if wrong, and accept that loss; entry tactics (breakouts vs pullbacks) change with the market, risk management never does.
Use hard stop orders and risk a small fixed fraction per trade (not 5%, more like ~0.3%, less than 0.5%) so that even 10 years out you haven't gone bankrupt.
Watch the leading index/leader (NVDA) at the declining EMAs: if it rejects the 50 EMA and can't reclaim/hold the 9 EMA while semis show relative strength, that's a bad sign for the whole market.
Don't rush; when many stocks sit under resistance/EMAs, wait for the close of today or tomorrow to decide direction. The close is crucial for deciding whether to be aggressive long.
Sector strength is a sufficient but not necessary factor for picking a stock; relative strength in the weekly big picture can justify a name even without sector confirmation.

Position count and exposure depend on (1) how much profit cushion existing positions give and (2) where the market is in its trend (start vs extended); don't take many new positions when the market is extended.
Avoid taking short entries while the market is gapping down / already falling, even when speculative leaders are bear-flagging and breaking down.
The technical setup is secondary; the most important factor is the big picture — is the stock gaining momentum, building higher lows, moving fast enough, and trading liquid enough.
The best breakouts come from huge, long bases (weeks, months, years); a multi-year base building higher lows with a tightening VCP is the highest-conviction structure.

When the market only just reclaims the 9 but is still under the 21 and individual stocks are loose, don't aggressively enter new positions; you're not out of the woods and a reversal is still possible.
Develop 'sit-down power' — learn to do nothing and wait rather than force trades in an indecisive market.
Trade liquid names (~$100M+ daily dollar volume): more liquidity means tighter spreads, less slippage, and easier execution.
Sell some into strength on the way up, and when the broad market is very extended don't bother trailing with the EMAs for a longer hold — close early rather than give back too much profit.
You don't need to know the catalyst; the price action going up is the most important thing to know.
